```{r, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>")
```

```{r setup}
library(must)
```

Calling a combined effect additive, synergistic or antagonistic is a
statement about a null model, not about the data alone. must separates the
three decisions behind such a statement and makes each one visible in the
output:

1. **What the design can identify** (`describe_design()`): which treatment
   combinations exist, which interactions they identify, which cells are
   shared, how the experimental units were replicated and sampled, and
   whether some stressor was applied to whole groups of units.
2. **Which model fits the data** (`fit_responses()`): a generalised linear
   mixed model per response, with its error distribution chosen for the
   data and not for the null model.
3. **What "non-additive" means** (`estimate_interactions()`): simple
   addition (AD), multiplication (MU) or dominance (DO), each on its own
   scale, tested from the predictions of the same model (Madge Pimentel et
   al. 2025), with a correction for experiments with few replicates.

## A worked example: insecticide, herbicide and nutrients

`polazzo_zooplankton` comes from an outdoor mesocosm experiment with a full
factorial of chlorpyrifos, diuron and nutrient enrichment, three mesocosms
per combination (Polazzo & Rico 2021). Zooplankton were sampled five days
before the pesticide application and on days 7, 14, 30 and 50 after it.
Because nutrient additions started four weeks before the pesticides, day -5
is not a pre-treatment baseline for all stressors; the example uses the four
samplings after the application.

```{r data}
zoo <- polazzo_zooplankton[polazzo_zooplankton$day > 0, ]
head(zoo)
```

### 1. The design

```{r example-design}
design <- describe_design(
  zoo,
  stressors = c("insecticide", "herbicide", "nutrients"),
  control = c(insecticide = "absent", herbicide = "absent", nutrients = "ambient"),
  unit = "mesocosm",
  time = "day"
)
design
design$sets[, c("set_id", "stressors", "net_identifiable", "pure_identifiable", "shared")]
```

The full factorial identifies the three pairwise interactions and both the
net deviation and the pure interaction of the three stressors. All four sets
share the control, and the mesocosms are measured repeatedly.

### 2. One model per response

Each response gets the candidates that suit its values (here positive
densities, with zeros for *Daphnia*); the one selected is the one with the
lowest AIC among those that converge and, by default, pass the DHARMa
residual checks. The checks are switched off here only because the vignette
must build without DHARMa.

```{r example-fit}
fits <- fit_responses(zoo, c("total_density", "cyclopoida", "daphnia"), design,
                      residual_checks = FALSE, seed = 1, quiet = TRUE)
fits
fits$fits$total_density$selection[, c("family", "link", "converged", "aic", "selected")]
fits$fits$daphnia$reason
```

*Daphnia* was absent from every mesocosm of some treatment combinations on
some days. With a log link their means lie on the boundary of the parameter
space, where intervals from the model are not valid, so they are fixed there.
When such a combination is the one a contrast compares with its reference
(the herbicide alone against the control, say), the contrast is tested from
the probability of observing only zeros if the null model held
(`status = "boundary"`); when it is a cell the null model needs to compute
its expectation, the contrast is `not_estimable`.

### 3. Null models

```{r example-estimate}
est <- estimate_interactions(fits, n_sim = 4000, seed = 2021)
e <- est$estimates
triple <- e[e$response == "total_density" & e$order == 3L & e$component == "interaction" &
              e$null_model != "DO",
            c("time", "null_model", "estimand", "estimate", "lower", "upper", "df",
              "p_value", "p_adjusted", "status")]
triple
```

On day 7 the net deviation of the three stressors is negative under AD and
MU, while the pure three-way interaction is not: the deviation is carried by
the pairwise interactions, which the full factorial lets us estimate. After
the adjustment for the many sets and times tested, neither is significant
with 24 mesocosms. The rows with `time = "overall"` average each effect over
the four samplings.

```{r example-pairs}
pairs7 <- e[e$response == "total_density" & e$time == "7" & e$order == 2L &
              e$component == "interaction" & e$null_model != "DO",
            c("stressors", "null_model", "estimate", "lower", "upper", "p_adjusted")]
pairs7
summary(est)
```

### 4. Classes

```{r example-classify}
cls <- classify_interactions(est)
table(cls$class, cls$order, useNA = "ifany")
cls[cls$response == "total_density" & cls$time == "7" & cls$null_model == "AD",
    c("stressors", "pattern", "class", "borderline")]
```

With the correction for small samples and the adjustment for multiple tests,
no interaction of this experiment deviates clearly from the null models.

```{r example-plot, fig.width = 7, fig.height = 4}
plot(est, response = "total_density", null_model = "MU")
```

## Few replicates: the small-sample correction

Madge Pimentel et al. (2025) obtain the uncertainty of the null-model
contrasts by simulating the fixed effects from a normal distribution with
their estimated covariance (Krinsky & Robb 1986). With the replication of
most mesocosm experiments that is too optimistic: the variance is estimated
by maximum likelihood, which underestimates it with few degrees of freedom,
and the normal ignores the uncertainty of that estimate. In simulated 2 x 2
experiments with three replicates per combination, the asymptotic tests
rejected a true null model in 10–17% of the cases instead of 5%. By default
(`correction = "small_sample"`) must refits the selected model by REML and
draws from a multivariate t whose degrees of freedom follow the experimental
units (column `df`). For a Gaussian model without random effects the AD
intervals of the delta method are then exactly those of `lm()`, and the
simulation approximates them:

```{r correction}
small <- data.frame(
  salinity = rep(c("ambient", "high", "ambient", "high"), each = 3),
  warming = rep(c("no", "no", "yes", "yes"), each = 3),
  growth = c(10.2, 9.1, 10.9, 8.3, 7.4, 8.8, 7.1, 6.0, 7.6, 3.2, 4.6, 3.9)
)
small$jar <- seq_len(nrow(small))
small_design <- describe_design(small, c("salinity", "warming"),
  control = c(salinity = "ambient", warming = "no"), unit = "jar")
small_fit <- fit_responses(small, "growth", small_design,
  families = list(gaussian = gaussian()), residual_checks = FALSE, seed = 1, quiet = TRUE)
interaction_row <- function(x) {
  x$estimates[x$estimates$component == "interaction",
              c("estimate", "lower", "upper", "df", "p_value")]
}
rbind(
  delta = interaction_row(estimate_interactions(small_fit, null_models = "AD",
                                                inference = "delta")),
  simulation = interaction_row(estimate_interactions(small_fit, null_models = "AD",
                                                     n_sim = 20000, seed = 1)),
  asymptotic = interaction_row(estimate_interactions(small_fit, null_models = "AD",
                                                     n_sim = 20000, seed = 1,
                                                     correction = "none"))
)
reference <- lm(growth ~ salinity * warming, data = small)
confint(reference)[4, ]
summary(reference)$coefficients[4, "Pr(>|t|)"]
```

With repeated measures or subsamples the degrees of freedom are those of the
units (units minus treatment combinations), and for stressors applied to
whole groups of units, those of the groups. Poisson and binomial models
without random effects have no variance to estimate and keep the normal
distribution. `correction = "none"` gives the asymptotic procedure, for
comparison with published analyses.

## Interactions in the presence of other stressors

By default each interaction is estimated with the stressors outside the set
at control: the insecticide × herbicide interaction compares mesocosms
without added nutrients. With `background = "all"` the design also gives the
same interaction in the presence of each level of the other stressors, with
that background as the reference:

```{r background}
design_all <- describe_design(zoo, c("insecticide", "herbicide", "nutrients"),
  control = c(insecticide = "absent", herbicide = "absent", nutrients = "ambient"),
  unit = "mesocosm", time = "day", background = "all")
design_all$sets[, c("set_id", "stressors", "background")]
```

## When an increase means sensitivity

MU and DO describe mechanisms (independent action, dominance of the
strongest stressor) only when an increase in the response means tolerance:
survival rather than mortality, abundance rather than damage. For responses
measured the other way, give their names in `sensitivity`: binomial
responses (successes out of `trials`, see `fit_responses()`) are then
analysed as their complement, and for other responses MU and DO are reported
as `not_applicable`.

```{r sensitivity}
jars <- data.frame(
  copper = rep(c("no", "yes", "no", "yes"), each = 5),
  heat = rep(c("no", "no", "yes", "yes"), each = 5),
  dead = c(1, 0, 1, 2, 1, 3, 2, 4, 3, 3, 2, 3, 2, 1, 2, 8, 9, 10, 9, 9),
  n = 10
)
jars$jar <- seq_len(nrow(jars))
jar_design <- describe_design(jars, c("copper", "heat"),
  control = c(copper = "no", heat = "no"), unit = "jar")
jar_fit <- fit_responses(jars, "dead", jar_design, trials = c(dead = "n"),
  residual_checks = FALSE, seed = 1, quiet = TRUE)
mortality <- estimate_interactions(jar_fit, n_sim = 4000, seed = 1, sensitivity = "dead")
mortality$estimates[mortality$estimates$component == "interaction",
                    c("null_model", "estimate", "lower", "upper", "p_value", "note")]
```

## What a design can and cannot identify

A design identifies an interaction only if it contains the control, each
stressor alone and their combination. Many experiments are not full
factorials. In a ray design, for example, two compounds are tested alone at
three doses and the mixture only at matching doses:

```{r ray}
ray <- data.frame(
  fungicide = c(0, 2, 20, 200, 0, 0, 0, 2, 20, 200),
  insecticide = c(0, 0, 0, 0, 2, 20, 200, 2, 20, 200)
)
ray <- ray[rep(seq_len(nrow(ray)), each = 3), ]
ray$mesocosm <- seq_len(nrow(ray))
ray_design <- describe_design(
  ray,
  stressors = c("fungicide", "insecticide"),
  control = c(fungicide = "0", insecticide = "0"),
  unit = "mesocosm"
)
ray_design
ray_design$sets[, c("set_id", "levels", "net_identifiable", "shared")]
```

Only the three diagonal combinations are identifiable, and all three share
the same control: their interaction estimates are correlated, so finding the
same class at the three doses is not three independent confirmations.

### Units inside groups: blocks, whole plots and confounding

A stressor is often applied to whole groups of units: one temperature per
climate room, one nitrate level per header tank, CO2 per plot. Then the
replication of that stressor is the number of groups, not of jars or
mesocosms. `groups` tells `describe_design()` which columns group the units.
Here temperature is applied to whole rooms and nutrients vary within them:

```{r rooms}
rooms <- expand.grid(temperature = c("15", "20"), room_rep = 1:2,
                     nutrients = c("no", "yes"), jar = 1:3, stringsAsFactors = FALSE)
rooms$room <- paste0("R", rooms$temperature, "-", rooms$room_rep)
rooms$jar_id <- seq_len(nrow(rooms))
one_room <- rooms[rooms$room_rep == 1, ]
one_design <- describe_design(
  one_room,
  stressors = c("temperature", "nutrients"),
  control = c(temperature = "15", nutrients = "no"),
  unit = "jar_id", groups = "room"
)
one_design$groups[, c("group", "between", "structure", "groups_per_combination", "random")]
one_design$sets[, c("stressors", "net_identifiable", "confounded")]
```

With one room per temperature, every effect of temperature, its interaction
with nutrients included, is also a difference between two rooms: the set is
`confounded`, and its estimates and class carry that flag. A random intercept
for rooms cannot separate them (its variance is not identifiable), so none is
added. With two rooms per temperature the rooms are whole plots: temperature
effects are replicated by rooms, and `fit_responses()` adds a random
intercept for them by default.

```{r rooms-replicated}
two_design <- describe_design(
  rooms,
  stressors = c("temperature", "nutrients"),
  control = c(temperature = "15", nutrients = "no"),
  unit = "jar_id", groups = "room"
)
two_design$groups[, c("group", "between", "structure", "groups_per_combination", "random")]
```

Blocks that hold every treatment combination (`structure = "blocks"`) also
get a random intercept. The design cannot reveal groups that are not in the
data: a shared incubator or water supply must be recorded to be checked.

## Three or more stressors: net deviation and pure interaction

With three stressors, the deviation of ABC from the combination of the
single effects (the **net** deviation) includes the pairwise interactions
AB, AC and BC. The **pure** third-order interaction is what remains once
those are removed, and it needs all eight combinations. In this simulated
2 x 2 x 2 experiment the pure interaction is negative, but part of the net
deviation comes from the pairwise terms:

```{r three-way}
grid <- expand.grid(nitrate = c("ambient", "high"), sediment = c("no", "yes"),
                    flow = c("normal", "low"), stringsAsFactors = FALSE)
n <- grid$nitrate == "high"
s <- grid$sediment == "yes"
f <- grid$flow == "low"
grid$mean <- 20 - 3 * n - 4 * s - 2 * f + 1.5 * n * s - n * f + 0.5 * s * f -
  2.5 * n * s * f
streams <- grid[rep(seq_len(8), each = 4), ]
streams$biomass <- streams$mean * rep(c(0.95, 1.02, 0.98, 1.05), 8)
streams$channel <- seq_len(nrow(streams))
stream_design <- describe_design(
  streams,
  stressors = c("nitrate", "sediment", "flow"),
  control = c(nitrate = "ambient", sediment = "no", flow = "normal"),
  unit = "channel"
)
stream_fit <- fit_responses(streams, "biomass", stream_design,
  families = list(gaussian = gaussian()), residual_checks = FALSE, quiet = TRUE)
stream_est <- estimate_interactions(stream_fit, null_models = "AD",
  inference = "delta")
int <- stream_est$estimates[stream_est$estimates$component == "interaction", ]
int[, c("stressors", "estimand", "estimate", "lower", "upper")]
```

The net deviation of the triple equals its pure interaction plus the three
pairwise interactions. If the design lacked the pairwise combinations, the
pure interaction would be reported as `not_identifiable` and
`describe_design()` would warn that the net deviation cannot be split.

## Decisions and their arguments

| Decision | Argument | Default |
|---|---|---|
| Level that means "no stressor" | `control` in `describe_design()` | none (required) |
| Experimental unit | `unit` | each row |
| Pre-treatment samplings | `baseline` | none |
| Groups of units (blocks, whole plots, rooms) | `groups` | none |
| Other stressors in each interaction | `background` | at control |
| Candidate error distributions | `families`, `response_types` | chosen from the values of each response |
| Successes out of a number of trials | `trials` | none |
| Sampling effort | `offset` | none |
| One dispersion for all, per `by` group or per combination | `dispersion` | `"common"` |
| Treatment effects constant over time? | `time_structure` | `"interaction"` (not constant) |
| Random effects | `random` | intercept per estimable group and per unit when units repeat; removed if its variance is estimated at zero |
| Optimiser limits | `control` | 20 iterations and 30 evaluations per fixed effect |
| Residual checks in the selection | `residual_checks` | `TRUE` (needs DHARMa) |
| Null models | `null_models` | AD, MU and DO |
| Uncertainty | `inference`, `n_sim` | Krinsky–Robb simulation, 10000 draws |
| Small-sample correction | `correction` | REML and t distribution |
| Responses where more means worse | `sensitivity` | none |
| Averages over times | `overall` | `TRUE` |
| Multiple testing | `p_adjust` | Benjamini–Hochberg |
| Random numbers | `seed` | drawn and stored in `settings$seed` |

## What a class means

`classify_interactions()` follows Table 1 of Piggott et al. (2015) under AD
and MU. For three or more stressors the same rules are applied to the net
deviation and its k single effects, a generalization made by this package.
"AD" means that no deviation was detected, not that additivity was shown;
under MU, synergism and antagonism are relative to the multiplicative
expectation. `borderline = TRUE` marks classes whose adjusted p-values are
so close to `alpha` that another seed could change them. MU and DO only
represent their mechanistic assumptions when an increase in the response
means tolerance (survival, abundance), and AD can predict impossible
negative values (flagged as `expected_below_zero`), in which case a deviation
from it says little about the mechanism (Madge Pimentel et al. 2025).
